title: "database is locked" migrating to 2.0
body: I get a database lock error when trying to migrate Syncthing to v2.0.0-rc.24 on Linux AMD64 with Docker Compose. Syncthing reports `Failed to migrate old-style database (error="openbase: runscripts: database is locked")`, exits with status 1, and starts again.

symptoms_visible: When I start Syncthing v2.0.0-rc.24 in Docker Compose, it reports `Failed to migrate old-style database` with `openbase: runscripts: database is locked`, exits with status 1, and starts again.
N0.label: N0 migration fails with locked database

symptoms_visible: The v2 migration still produces the database lock error in my Proxmox Debian VM.
After temporarily changing config.xml to version 37, my existing service works again without completing the v2 migration.
N1.label: N1 deployment described and migration bypassed

symptoms_visible: The v2 database migration has not completed; I am still using the temporary config.xml version change.
Inside the container, my lsof command lists only the BusyBox shell descriptors, while top lists two `/bin/syncthing` processes with PIDs 19882 and 1.
N2.label: N2 open-process probe collected

symptoms_visible: After moving my configuration files to a Docker volume and deploying the v2 container, the migration completes as expected.
N3.label: N3 migration succeeds after storage move

symptoms_visible: Syncthing v2 starts successfully after I copy the existing v1.30 configuration from the bind mount into Docker-managed storage.
The database migration completes and all my settings are preserved.
N4.label: N4 successful storage procedure clarified

symptoms_visible: Syncthing v2 starts normally with its configuration and database in local Docker storage; the migration finishes without the database lock error and my existing settings remain available.
N_terminal.label: terminal migration completed with local database storage

question_patterns: Can you describe the host, VM, operating system, and container image in this setup?
What does your Docker deployment run on?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: It runs under Proxmox 8.4 in a Debian Trixie VM, using the official Syncthing Docker image from the Trixie Docker distribution.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: This is not Docker at all; it is a native Syncthing process directly on macOS.

question_patterns: Which Syncthing version were you upgrading from?
What was the last version that used this database successfully?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I believe I tried to move from v1.30 to v2.0.0-rc.24, although I have some doubt whether the original version was v1.30 or the version just before it.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The source was the release immediately before v1.30 rather than exactly v1.30.

question_patterns: How has this container been maintained or updated over time?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I have updated the container at almost every release since early 2023 using the latest tag.

question_patterns: Is there anything else notable in front of or around the container?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I use Traefik in front of it, but otherwise it is an alone service and there is nothing special.

edges.comment: Issue c0-c1, reporter's system only: the maintainer asks for deployment details. In the same reply, the reporter independently states that changing config.xml to v37 temporarily made the existing service work again; that persistent workaround is recorded in N1.volunteered_info.

question_patterns: Can you run lsof on the database path and paste the raw output?
Please check which processes are present while investigating the locked database and show the command output.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I ran `lsof /config/config/index-v0.14.0.db/current`. It printed four entries for PID 28463 `/bin/busybox`, attached to `/dev/pts/0` and `/dev/tty`. In `top`, I see `/bin/syncthing` as PID 19882 with PPID 1 and another `/bin/syncthing` as PID 1, plus my shell and top.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: lsof clearly lists a separate container process holding the database files open after the Syncthing container is stopped.
The same shell and Syncthing entries appear with different process IDs.

edges.comment: Issue c3-c6, reporter's system only: another participant raises the possibility of another process and requests lsof output. The reporter supplies raw lsof and top results but does not identify which process, if any, owns the database lock; no engineer conclusion is placed in the user's answer.

solution.intent: Preserve the existing Syncthing configuration while testing whether moving the configuration and database from their current storage into Docker-managed local volumes allows the v2 migration to complete.
solution.concrete_example: Create Docker volumes for the Syncthing configuration, copy the existing configuration into them, point the container at those volumes, and retry the v2 start instead of deleting the settings.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter independently tried moving the configuration files and observed that migration then succeeded. That comparison implicates the original storage arrangement, but it does not by itself establish the exact filesystem-locking mechanism or prove that another process held the database.

edges.comment: Issue c7, reporter's system only: the reporter independently moves the configuration files to Docker volume storage and confirms that the v2 migration occurs as expected. This is the persistent system change from S1b to S2.

question_patterns: What exactly was the previous storage method that failed?
When you said the files were stored using another method, did you mean a bind mount, a network mount, or something else?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The term I could not remember was bind mounts. My existing Syncthing configuration files had been stored in a bind mount before I moved them.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The database was already in the same local Docker volume before and after the test; only the container image changed.
The old storage was a different local bind-mounted directory on the same host.

question_patterns: Which container paths did you put on Docker volumes?
Can you clarify which paths now use Docker volumes?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I use one volume for `/config` and another one for `/var/syncthing`.

question_patterns: What exact sequence did you use to move the existing installation without losing its configuration?
Did you copy the old configuration into the new volume before starting v2?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I created Docker volumes, copied the existing v1.30 configuration files from my bind mount into the new volume, changed Docker Compose to point Syncthing at that volume, changed the container to v2, and started it. The migration completed and all my settings were preserved.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: I deleted the old configuration and created a completely new Syncthing identity; no database migration actually ran.

edges.comment: Issue c8-c12, reporter's system only: after the successful migration, the reporter is asked to define the previous 'another method' and gives the precise bind-mount-to-volume procedure. Settings preservation is an additional fact volunteered in that answer and is recorded in N4.

solution.intent: Keep Syncthing's configuration database on storage local to the machine running Syncthing, while allowing separately mounted locations to hold folders that Syncthing synchronizes.
solution.concrete_example: Place the configuration/database path in a local Docker volume or local host directory, copy the existing configuration into it, and mount any NAS-backed folders at separate paths as synchronized data rather than as the database location.
solution.inference_hint: The thread's accepted operational guidance is that the Syncthing database belongs on the machine where Syncthing runs. The original reporter established only that a bind-mount-to-Docker-volume move fixed their migration; they did not establish that their bind mount was SMB/NFS or identify a precise lock implementation failure. Later users separately reported network-backed mounts, so those setups must not be retroactively attributed to this reporter.

edges.comment: Technical resolution synthesized from reporter c7-c12 and maintainer c18. The reporter personally verified successful migration with preserved settings. The later SMB/CIFS deployments belong to other participants and support the general local-database guidance, but their storage details are not inserted into the reporter's causal history.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify storage placement as the decisive issue established for this case: the migration failed with the configuration database on the reporter's bind-mounted storage and succeeded after the existing configuration was copied to Docker-managed storage.
Must recommend keeping the Syncthing configuration database local to the machine running Syncthing; remote or NAS-backed locations may be mounted separately for folders being synchronized.

Must not overclaim that the original reporter proved an SMB, CIFS, NFS, POSIX-locking, permissions, UID, or second-process root cause; the thread does not establish the exact underlying mechanism for that reporter.
Must not require deleting the existing configuration or starting from scratch, because copying the existing files preserved the reporter's settings and allowed migration.
Must ground the recommendation in the successful bind-mount-to-volume comparison rather than treating the raw lsof/top output as proof of another process holding the database.
Must have the user verify that v2 starts, completes the migration without the lock error, and retains the existing settings before declaring resolution.

persona_hint.experience_level: Docker Compose user with practical self-hosting experience but limited familiarity with Linux process and storage diagnostics; can edit XML and Compose files, move persistent data, and run commands when given exact instructions.
persona_hint.communication_style: Polite, concise, and cooperative; openly states uncertainty, follows concrete commands, and later documents the successful migration procedure step by step.
